title: The written mandala
hook: Nichiren's scroll, inscribed with the title and the names of Buddhas

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nichiren schools, and a chant that is really a book's title. Your line was the title. Which name did you say on purpose? Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

Open the doors of the small cabinet, and there is no statue inside. There is a sheet of paper, mounted as a scroll. Down the middle runs a column of large, bold brushstrokes. Around it, smaller columns of characters spread out toward the edges, like a crowd gathered around a speaker. Some of the marks near the sides look less like writing and more like drawing. People bow to this paper. They chant facing it. They dust the cabinet that holds it. Today's word is the name of that scroll: gohonzon.
screen: `NO STATUE INSIDE.` → `A COLUMN OF BOLD STROKES.` → `A CROWD OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. Gohonzon means, roughly, the object of devotion, said with respect. Nichiren inscribed scrolls like this by hand and gave them to his followers. Where other temples carved or painted the Buddha, he wrote. That is why some call it a written mandala: a sacred diagram made of words instead of pictures. Second, the center. Down the middle, in the largest letters, runs the title we met yesterday, namu myoho renge kyo, with Nichiren's own signature written below it. The title is the heart of the scroll, just as it is the heart of the chant. Third, everything around it. The Lotus Sutra tells of a great jeweled tower that rises out of the earth and hangs in the air. Inside sits a Buddha from an age long past, and Shakyamuni Buddha sits down beside him, while a vast assembly gathers to listen. The gohonzon is often read as that scene, written out: the names of two Buddhas on either side of the title, and around them bodhisattvas, disciples, gods and guardians, and even beings from the dark and troubled corners of existence. Even the dark corners have a place on the page. Fourth, how people use it. Practitioners chant facing the gohonzon, often morning and evening. Some communities describe it as a kind of mirror: chanting before it, a person is meant to see their own capacity for awakening reflected back. Communities differ, sometimes deeply, about which scrolls are authentic and who may give them out, and that is tomorrow's story. But the scroll is handled with care: kept clean, set up high, never tossed aside. In these homes, what sits at the center of the room is a sheet of paper covered in writing.
screen: `WRITING INSTEAD OF A STATUE.` · `THE TITLE DOWN THE CENTER.` · `THE WHOLE ASSEMBLY AROUND IT.` · `A MIRROR, KEPT WITH CARE.` · then, large: `THE SCROLL.`

segments.voice: If there is a sacred scroll, verse or image where you live, sit facing it. If not, any page of writing that matters to you will do: a letter, a card, a line someone wrote for you. Look at it without reading it. See the shapes of the letters. Notice where your eye lands first, what sits at the center, and what sits out at the edges. Then close your eyes and keep the picture in mind. Ask quietly what you would place at the center of your own page. The bell holds the time.
Gohonzon. The scroll Nichiren inscribed, with the Lotus Sutra's title down the center and the names of Buddhas and many beings around it, faced in chanting. Today's word.
Your line: the scroll. Today, look at one thing hanging on a wall you pass every day, and ask what it puts at the center. Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Nichiren Buddhists enshrine a gohonzon, a scroll with the Lotus Sutra's title down the center and the names of Buddhas and other beings around it, and chant facing it, often morning and evening, at home and in temples.

a scene from the Lotus Sutra

fork.setup: you're Nichiren. your followers need something to face when they chant. what do you make for them?
options: a carved statue of the Buddha.
a painting of the jeweled tower.
a scroll of written names around the title.
fork.reveal: he writes. the scroll puts the title at the center and the whole assembly of the jeweled tower around it, in words instead of pictures.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Japanese scroll is calligraphy for decoration.
what it means: the gohonzon is an object of devotion, the Lotus Sutra's title down the center, faced in chanting.
what a scholar hears: a written mandala of the jeweled-tower assembly from the Lotus Sutra, two Buddhas beside the title and every kind of being around it.

sources.work: the writings and scrolls of Nichiren

notes: Gloss of gohonzon as 'the object of devotion, said with respect' (go- honorific + honzon): confirm.
Reading the gohonzon as the Ceremony in the Air / Treasure Tower assembly, with Shakyamuni and Many Treasures (Prabhutaratna) beside the title: standard in Nichiren teaching, but confirm wording.
The 'marks that look like drawing' are the Siddham seed syllables for Fudo and Aizen found on many gohonzon; not named in the voice, confirm the hook's description.
The mirror image is attributed to 'some communities' (it is common in Soka Gakkai teaching); confirm.
'Often morning and evening' (gongyo) and 'kept up high': confirm as fair descriptions across communities.
Communities differ on authenticity and conferral of gohonzon; deliberately left for the next day.

Editor: cut the count-like 'on many scrolls' (now 'Nichiren's own signature written below it'; confirm), 'a couple of the marks' became 'some of the marks', and the sweeping 'nobody is left off the page' became 'even the dark corners have a place on the page' in voice and myth.
